title: Maharashtra Farmers to Get Rs 5,000 Advance as Drought Relief
excerpt: Cabinet approves Rs 7,500 crore for 1.5 crore farmers before Diwali, with banks told not to deduct dues and full crop-loss compensation to follow field surveys
body:
• Maharashtra will pay an advance of Rs 5,000 to each of about 1.5 crore farmers, a total outlay of Rs 7,500 crore, with transfers directed this week before Diwali.
  • Banks have been told not to deduct any amount from the payments; the advance is separate from crop-loss compensation, which will be set after panchnama field surveys.
  • Drought has been declared in 305 of the state's 358 talukas; compensation norms range from Rs 7,500 to Rs 22,000 per hectare, so the final payment for many farmers will exceed the advance.
  • Farmer groups marching on Mumbai call Rs 5,000 inadequate and want a written commitment on aid, loan waiver and crop insurance.

Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis has directed officials to deposit Rs 5,000 each as advance drought relief into the bank accounts of about 1.5 crore farmers this week, with a total provision of Rs 7,500 crore, according to reports of a state Cabinet decision on Tuesday. Fadnavis also instructed officials to issue explicit directions to banks so that no amount is deducted from the payments against outstanding dues.

Deputy Chief Minister Eknath Shinde said the money would reach farmers before Diwali. "A provision of Rs 7,500 crore has been made; the money will be transferred to their accounts immediately. Farmers will get money before Diwali. We will not let farmers' Diwali turn dark," Shinde said.

What farmers will receive, and what comes later

The Rs 5,000 is an advance, not the final settlement. Shinde said farmers will also receive the 12 kinds of benefits that follow a drought declaration, including fee waivers, water arrangements, loan reorganisation and easier loan recovery, in addition to the cash payment. Fadnavis said every eligible farmer will receive at least Rs 5,000, with the remaining compensation paid later.

That later payment depends on panchnamas, the field surveys that record crop damage. Under compensation norms adopted in 2023, crop-loss payment ranges from Rs 7,500 to Rs 22,000 per hectare depending on the crop. A farmer with two hectares assessed at the lowest rate would be due Rs 15,000, three times the advance. No date for the crop-loss payment order has been given in the reports.

Fadnavis, speaking in Wardha on Sunday, said this was the first time the state had paid advance assistance before December, and that smallholders previously received barely Rs 1,000. "Rs 5,000 cannot compensate for their losses, but it will offer some relief," he said, contrasting the payment with Karnataka's Rs 2,500.

Scale of the drought

The state first declared drought in 265 talukas across 32 districts on September 26 and added 40 more in October, taking the total to 305 of 358 talukas. Between June 1 and September 26, Maharashtra received 798.2 mm of rain against an average of 970.9 mm, a shortfall of 18 percent. Marathwada recorded a deficit of 38 percent across its eight districts, and Vidarbha averaged a 27 percent deficit across 11 districts.

The declaration triggers land revenue waivers, crop loan restructuring, deferred recovery, power bill concessions, exam fee waivers, relaxed employment guarantee rules and water tankers where needed. The state has also sought central assistance: on October 7, Fadnavis handed Union Home Minister Amit Shah an interim proposal for Rs 17,500 crore, comprising Rs 13,000 crore for crop losses and Rs 4,500 crore for fodder. An 11-member central team has toured the affected areas.

Farmers' groups say the advance is too small

The announcement has not ended pressure on the government. More than 12,000 farmers and rural workers led by the All India Kisan Sabha began a march from Akole on October 26 toward Varsha, the chief minister's official residence in Mumbai, demanding higher drought relief, faster crop insurance payments and a wider loan waiver. The Kisan Sabha has called the Rs 5,000 payment too little and has asked for a formal written commitment on each demand, saying the protest will continue until it receives one.

The marchers also want the Rs 2 lakh loan waiver extended to farmers who repay regularly, release of two pending Namo Shetkari instalments (Rs 6,000 a year in three instalments), and ownership rights over forest, temple trust, inam and grazing land. Fadnavis was expected to meet a delegation on Tuesday evening.

What happens next

The immediate test is delivery: whether the Rs 5,000 reaches 1.5 crore accounts before Diwali without bank deductions. Beyond that, the size and timing of crop-loss compensation will be set by the panchnama surveys and the Centre's response to the Rs 17,500 crore request.
